                                    EXPLANATORY STATEMENT


     PRIMA has proven to be an effective framework for fostering scientific cooperation in the
     Mediterranean, addressing pressing challenges such as integrated water management. The
     interim evaluation of 2023 confirmed its added value, demonstrating that it strengthens
     research capacities and supports the Union’s strategic priorities in the region.

     In particular, PRIMA has proven to be a model of science diplomacy in the Mediterranean, a
     region of geopolitical importance for the Union. The partnership operates on the principles of
     mutual benefit, equal footing, co-ownership, co-decision and co-financing. Addressing the
     critical challenges of the region, where 180 million people are considered 'water poor',
     PRIMA's work directly contributes to regional stability, prosperity and resilience. The
     programme follows a long-term Strategic Research and Innovation Agenda covering three
     interconnected thematic areas: water management, farming systems and the food value chain,
     integrated since 2019 through the innovative Water-Energy-Food-Ecosystems Nexus
     approach.

     The Kingdom of Morocco has been a committed partner in PRIMA since its inception. The
     amended agreement aligns its participation with the new terms introduced under Horizon
     Europe and ensures compliance with the updated legal and financial framework. This step
     will allow Morocco to remain fully engaged in the partnership until 2031, guaranteeing
     continuity of cooperation and joint work on shared challenges.

     The agreement is consistent with the EU’s external policies, including the New Agenda for
     the Mediterranean, the Global Approach to Research and Innovation and the Union’s
     development objectives. It carries no additional budgetary implications beyond those already
     foreseen in the continuation of PRIMA under Horizon Europe.

     In light of the above, Rapporteur believes that it is in the Union’s interest to conclude this
     agreement. This will ensure continuity of the partnership and strengthen the EU's engagement
     with the regional partner and reinforces the Union's commitment to addressing shared
     Mediterranean challenges through collaborative science, contributing simultaneously to
     research excellence, regional stability and development.

     However, it remains necessary to take into account the competitive pressure exerted by
     agricultural products from the third country on those produced in EU Member States.
     European producers are, in fact, subject to stricter regulations, particularly environmental
     ones, and consequently face higher production costs. Therefore, any form of cooperation,
     including the scientific cooperation under PRIMA, should be based on reciprocity and should
     ensure adequate safeguards for the agricultural sector.

     The Commission is therefore called upon to closely monitor the implementation of this
     agreement within the broader framework of EU-Morocco relations, in particular as regards the
     import of agricultural products into the Union, ensuring that appropriate safeguards are applied
     where necessary and that the principles of reciprocity and fair competition are upheld.

                                   EXPLANATORY STATEMENT


On 11 May 2024 the European Parliament and the Council signed a new Directive (EU)
2024/1203 of the European Parliament and of the Council2, replacing Directive 2008/99/EC of
the European Parliament and of the Council3, which had been widely considered ineffective.
To address shortcomings in the effectiveness of environmental criminal law, Directive (EU)
2024/1203 laid down minimum rules with regard to the definition of criminal offences and
penalties in order to protect the environment more effectively, as well as measures in order to
prevent and combat environmental crime.

Almost simultaneously with the EU procedure concerning Directive (EU) 2024/1203, the
Council of Europe (CoE) began work on a revised Convention on the Protection of the
Environment through Criminal Law4 (‘new Convention’) to replace the one dating back to
19985 (‘old Convention’). The old Convention was a pioneering instrument which was the first
international instrument containing definitions of the most serious environmental offences
committed intentionally or with negligence, as well as provisions on jurisdiction, effective and
dissuasive sanctions, confiscation measures, reinstatement of the environment, corporate
liability, cooperation between the parties to that convention and international cooperation, and
the rights for groups, foundations or associations which aim at the protection of the environment
to participate in criminal proceedings in accordance with domestic law.

On 3 April 2023 the CoE set up the Committee of Experts on the Protection of the Environment
through Criminal Law (PC-ENV). A draft of the new Convention was finalised on 9 October
2024. On 14 May 2025 the new Convention was adopted by the Committee of Ministers of the
CoE and opened for signature on 3 December 2025.

The Commission participated in the negotiations on the basis of Council Decision (EU)
2023/2170 of 28 September 20236. Following successful conclusion of the negotiations, the
Council adopted Council Decision (EU) 2025/2493 of 1 December 2025 on the signing, on
behalf of the European Union, of the CoE Convention on the Protection of the Environment

      through Criminal Law7. Subsequently, pursuant to Article 218 of the Treaty on the Functioning
     of the European Union, the Council requested the consent of the European Parliament to the

     According to the Commission’s assessment, the new Convention establishes binding
     international standards for defining and criminalising serious environmental
     offences punishable by effective, proportionate and dissuasive sanctions. It also strengthens
     prevention measures and international cooperation to address environmental crime, including
     through cross-border investigations, information exchange and the collection of statistical
     data. Upon its entry into force, neighbouring countries will apply criminal law standards
     consistent with those of the EU, thereby, in effect, improving cooperation, investigations and
     accountability. For EU Member States, the new Convention is consistent with Directive (EU)
     2024/1203, however they can go beyond the requirements of both that Directive and that
     Convention when implementing their provisions.

     The Convention is expected to enter into force upon ten ratifications, including at least eight
     ratifications by member States of CoE. Alongside CoE member States, the new Convention is
     open for signature by non-member States that have participated in its elaboration and the EU.

     In light of the above considerations, the Rapporteur fully recommends that the Parliament
     give its consent to the conclusion of the new Convention.

A.    whereas enlargement is a key EU foreign policy tool and a strategic geopolitical

                               EXPLANATORY STATEMENT


This draft report provides Parliament’s response to the 2025 Commission report on Serbia. It
reflects the events of the past year as well as more recent ones, including the Committee on
Foreign Affairs’ mission to Serbia from 22 to 24 January 2026.

Serbia has been an EU candidate country since 2012. Since accession negotiations with Serbia
began in January 2014, 22 out of 35 chapters have been opened. Serbia accepted the revised
enlargement methodology in June 2021, but has made no progress on opening new clusters
since December 2021.

In recent years, Serbia’s progress towards EU accession has stalled, with concerns
predominantly focused on the state of democracy and the rule of law. There are many urgent
issues to resolve, particularly heightened political polarisation and tensions, the need for
structural reforms addressing the rule of law, anti-corruption and other EU-related matters, and
the necessity of reaching a comprehensive normalisation agreement with Kosovo, while
achieving full alignment with EU foreign policy.

The draft report also addresses important issues regarding the independence of key institutions
and stresses the need to implement all outstanding commitments, including recommendations
on key aspects of the electoral process, in an inclusive and transparent manner.

     Progress with EU accession-related reforms, in particular on the rule of law and
     governance

     1.   Commends Moldova for its continued exemplary commitment to EU accession and its
          steadfast progress with related reforms despite significant internal and external
          challenges, such as persistent hostile Russian interference; welcomes the Commission’s
          assessment that Moldova made progress across all chapters and achieved the biggest
          annual progress among the candidate countries; considers this progress particularly
          remarkable given the extraordinary geopolitical pressure under which the country
          continues to operate; encourages Moldova to maintain the pace of reforms, so that
          progress translates into tangible benefits for citizens and businesses, strengthening
          economic development, resilience and convergence with the European Union in line
          with its stated ambition to provisionally close accession negotiations by early 2028;

     2.   Welcomes the successful completion of the bilateral screening process and the start of
          technical talks on the negotiation clusters; welcomes the Commission’s assessment that
          all six negotiation clusters are ready to be opened; urges the Council to take a merit-
          based approach and formally open the clusters without any further delay, starting with
          the fundamentals cluster; reminds the Member States of the principle of sincere
          cooperation under Article 4(3) of the Treaty on European Union, which requires them to

          objectives, and therefore urges them to avoid blocking or delaying accession
          negotiations based on bilateral issues; emphasises that opening accession negotiations

          reinforcing the credibility and integrity of the enlargement process; welcomes the
          adoption of road maps on the rule of law, on public administration and on democratic
          institutions, and the updated National Programme for Accession to the European Union
          for the period 2025–2029; commends the progress already achieved by Moldova at the
          technical level in the transposition of the EU acquis;

 3.    Underlines that the pace of the Moldova’s accession process should reflect the

      institutional reform, the rule of law, and sustainable economic development;

      the justice sector; reminds Moldova of its commitment to follow the recommendations
      of the Venice Commission; stresses that the sustainability of reforms requires broad
      political ownership and inclusive dialogue across the political spectrum, as well as
      meaningful consultation with civil society and professional stakeholders; recognises
      Moldova’s consistent political will and sustained efforts to build an independent,
      impartial, accountable and professional judicial system;

6.    Calls on the Moldovan authorities to ensure that the vetting process of judges and
      prosecutors is conducted in an inclusive, predictable and legally robust manner and
      encourages the country to effectively conclude the process without delay, as completing
      vetting is critical to ensuring public trust in the judiciary, eliminating compromised
      judges, and reinforcing the rule of law as a cornerstone for EU integration; calls on
      Moldova to ensure sufficient budgetary and human resources for judicial bodies and
      continue taking measures to strengthen their capacities in order, inter alia, to address the
      deficit of judges and prosecutors, reduce the length of proceedings, especially in
      corruption and economic crime cases, and improve the digitalisation, accessibility,
      efficiency and transparency of justice for all citizens;

      corruption, with its improved track record in both high-level and non-high-level cases;

      independence, professionalism and accountability, and enhance coordination
      mechanisms among all key anti-corruption and justice institutions, in order to guarantee

      undermine legal certainty and institutional trust; emphasises the importance of

      economic and media spheres remains a key priority for advancing Moldova’s European
      integration;

      consecutive vote confirming the support of the people of Moldova for the country’s EU
      accession and related reforms; strongly condemns the repeated attempts by the Russian

     While recognising the sovereign right of the Republic of Moldova to determine its own
     political and economic future and while supporting constructive relations between the
     European Union and Moldova, we do not share the report’s underlying assumption that EU
     membership constitutes the only or the most appropriate framework for cooperation.

     EU enlargement towards countries with unresolved territorial disputes, substantial economic
     disparities and significant dependence on external financial assistance, risks imposing new
     financial and political burdens on existing Member States. The accession process should not
     be driven by geopolitical considerations alone, nor should enlargement be presented as a
     strategic instrument in broader regional confrontations.

     We support a partnership with Moldova that can deliver tangible benefits to both sides
     without creating additional financial obligations for European taxpayers or further
     complicating the functioning of the Union.

     We advocate a model of cooperation and strategic partnership rather than full EU membership
     and consequently oppose the report.

                               EXPLANATORY STATEMENT




As rapporteur for this important initiative, I am pleased to present a report that reflects a
permanent and steadfast strategic commitment to Ukraine by the European Union. The report
takes stock of the state of play of the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine and EU long
term financial support as well as of EU sanctions regime and EU accession negotiations over
the last year. It reviews Ukraine's progress, against the backdrop of the ongoing war, in the
following areas: democracy and democratic institutions, rule of law and judicial reforms, fight
against corruption, fundamental freedoms and human rights, the role of civil society, single
market integration, defence cooperation with the EU, regional and good neighbourly relations,
socio-economic reforms, energy, transport and sustainable development. It praises where
possible and encourages where necessary. The reforms, which are the centre piece of the
report, are crucial for the preparation of Ukraine to meet the requirements of EU membership.
It is therefore imperative that in the lifecycle of this report the negotiations on EU accession
of Ukraine begin. In the amendments phase additional aspects and updates improved and
complimented the draft report

                                   EXPLANATORY STATEMENT


     The Protocol

     The Republic of Croatia joined the European Union on 1 July 2013. In accordance with the
     Act concerning the conditions of accession, Croatia has undertaken to accede to the
     agreements concluded or signed by the Member States and the Union with one or more third
     countries or an international organisation, including the Euro-Mediterranean Aviation
     Agreement with Morocco.

     The accession of Croatia to such agreements shall be agreed by the conclusion of a protocol to
     these agreements between the Council, acting unanimously on behalf of the Member States,
     and the third country or countries or international organisation concerned.

     The Commission has negotiated the Protocol amending the Euro-Mediterranean Aviation
     Agreement between the European Community and its Member States, of the one part, and the
     Kingdom of Morocco, of the other part. The Protocol defines the linguistic adaptations to be
     made to the Agreement by reason of the accession of Croatia.

     Rapporteur’s position

     The Agreement with Morocco was the first comprehensive air transport agreement signed
     with a non-EU partner of the Union. That Agreement is an important element of the Union’s
     external aviation policy and is one of several Euro-Mediterranean aviation agreements which
     the Union has since signed also with Israel and Jordan. The Aviation Agreement with
     Morocco has made it possible to nearly triple, in absolute terms, connectivity between that
     country and the Union.

     By granting all EU air carriers non-discriminatory access to routes between the EU and
     Morocco, this agreement promotes competition on air routes between the EU and an
     important EU partner in the Mediterranean and will, consequently, improve connectivity. This
     Protocol will enable Croatia to enjoy these benefits in the same way as the other Member
     States currently do.

     Based on all the above, the rapporteur recommends that the Committee on Transport and
     Tourism give its approval to the conclusion of this protocol.

     The Commission argues that this trade agreement will help Europe address geopolitical
     instability and economic uncertainty. But this deal will not deliver the benefits claimed.

     It gives corporations the right to sue States before international tribunals for millions of euros
     when governments regulate in the public interest, while granting no equivalent rights to
     workers, communities or the environment. This exposes a contradiction with Europe’s exit
     from the Energy Charter Treaty to protect itself from such lawsuits.

     The agreement also runs counter to efforts to re-industrialise Europe. It facilitates the
     relocation of industries, particularly automotive production, to Mexico, and puts workers in
     Europe and Mexico into competition instead of supporting decent jobs, deepening a race to
     the bottom.

     It restricts governments’ policy space while promoting a harmful extractivist model. It also
     incentivises agri-food exports instead of supporting agricultural sovereignty in Mexico and
     Europe.

     The Commission’s own evaluation of the existing agreement with Mexico found that, after
     nearly twenty years, its impact was marginal for both parties even by the narrow measure of
     GDP. There is little basis to expect this revised deal to deliver the promised economic
     benefits.

     We support a stronger EU-Mexico relationship and closer cooperation, but on different terms.

                                    EXPLANATORY STATEMENT


     The modernised EU–Mexico Global Agreement represents a major step forward in
     strengthening the strategic partnership between the European Union and one of its closest
     partners in Latin America. Building on the original agreement that entered into force in 2000,
     the updated framework reflects more than two decades of deepening political, economic and
     social ties and responds to the evolving geopolitical and economic realities facing both
     partners.

     Mexico is one of the European Union’s most strategic partners in the region. The EU is
     Mexico’s third-largest trading partner and a major source of foreign direct investment. Over
     the past twenty-five years, bilateral trade has grown substantially, demonstrating the mutual
     benefits of open, rules-based cooperation. The modernised agreement aims to consolidate and
     expand this relationship by updating the legal and institutional framework governing political
     dialogue, economic cooperation and trade relations.

     From a political perspective, the agreement reinforces the shared commitment of the EU and
     Mexico to multilateralism, and the rules-based international order. At a time of increasing
     geopolitical uncertainty and growing protectionist tendencies in parts of the world,
     strengthening partnerships with like-minded countries is of strategic importance. The
     agreement provides a platform to deepen cooperation on global challenges such as sustainable
     development, digital transformation and security. It also enhances political dialogue and
     cooperation across a wide range of policy areas, thereby strengthening the broader strategic
     partnership between the two sides.

     From an economic and trade perspective, the modernised agreement represents a significant
     upgrade of the trade pillar of the EU–Mexico relationship. The updated trade provisions aim
     to improve market access for goods and services, strengthen rules on public procurement and
     intellectual property, and provide a more predictable and transparent framework for
     businesses and investors. Importantly, the agreement also marks a milestone in EU trade
     policy as the first trade agreement to include a dedicated anti-corruption clause. Transparency,
     good governance and the fight against corruption are essential conditions for fair legal
     certainty and sustainable economic cooperation.

     The agreement is also expected to create new opportunities for European companies,
     including small and medium-sized enterprises, by reducing barriers to trade and investment
     and by facilitating participation in procurement markets. For European exporters and
     investors, Mexico represents a dynamic and growing economy with strong potential for
     further cooperation, particularly in sectors such as digital services, infrastructure and
     advanced manufacturing. At the same time, continued efforts to strengthen the rule of law and
     legal certainty will remain essential to ensuring a stable and predictable investment
     environment. With the signing of this agreement, total EU exports of goods and services
     could increase by 75% in the most ambitious scenario, and EU companies could save up to
     EUR 100 million per year in customs duties.

     The modernised Global Agreement strengthens the EU’s engagement with Latin America at a
     time when closer transatlantic cooperation is increasingly important. By deepening ties with
     Mexico, the EU reinforces its presence in the region and contributes to a more diversified and
     resilient network of international partnerships. The signing of this agreement demonstrates,

                                    MINORITY POSITION


                       pursuant to Rule 56(4) of the Rules of Procedure
                         Manon Aubry, Marina Mesure, Rudi Kennes


This deal is a corporate power-grab. It gives corporations the right to sue States before
international tribunals and claim millions of euros when governments regulate in the public
interest, while granting no equivalent enforceable rights to workers, communities or the
environment. This exposes a glaring contradiction with Europe’s exit from the Energy Charter
Treaty to protect itself from such lawsuits.
The agreement also runs counter to efforts to re-industrialise Europe. It facilitates the
relocation of industries, particularly automotive production, to Mexico, and puts workers in
Europe and Mexico into competition instead of supporting decent jobs, deepening a race to
the bottom in labour conditions.
It significantly restricts governments’ policy space while promoting a harmful extractivist
model and incentivises agri-food exports instead of supporting agricultural sovereignty.
This agreement will not deliver the benefits claimed. More than 95% of EU-Mexico trade in
goods has already been tariff-free for over a decade and the Commission’s own evaluation of
the existing agreement found that, after nearly twenty years, its economic impact was
marginal even by the narrow measure of GDP.
We support stronger EU–Mexico relations and closer cooperation but on different terms.
